items.title: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial
items.summary:
Exclusive: Jury was never told that Prof Peter Hindmarsh was barred from practising over concerns for patients’ safety

A senior doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby and who was held up by prosecutors as a pre-eminent expert was barred from treating patients during the trial over fears he posed a risk to their safety.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a specialist in hormones in children, was crucial to the crown’s argument that Letby had poisoned children by injecting insulin into fluid bags. But a Guardian investigation can reveal he was excluded from clinical practice in March 2023, five months before the end of the trial, by his employer, University College London hospitals trust (UCLH). Jurors were never told.

Continue reading...
items.t: Doctor whose evidence helped to convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during trial

Fears are growing that the US could impose sanctions on judges at the international court of justice, including this year’s Nobel peace prize winner, Navi Pillay, if the court rules on Thursday that the Myanmar government committed genocide against the Rohingya.

The ICJ has never found a state responsible for committing genocide, and a significant factor in previous cases has been how to prove “intent” in a crime defined as acts committed with the “intent to destroy, in whole or in part” a national, ethnical, racial or religious group.

items.title: Where The ‘Cravath Scale’ Actually Began
items.summary:
Ed. Note: Welcome to our daily feature Trivia Question of the Day! 

For generations, every Biglaw associate’s paycheck was measured against the “Cravath scale,” the lockstep benchmark that top firms race to match. It all traces to a single raise in 1968, when Cravath, Swaine & Moore “blew the ceiling off” the market by jumping its first-year starting salary to a then-shocking new figure, sending Wall Street firms scrambling to keep up. What was that 1968 starting salary, the number that launched the modern associate pay wars? 

Hint: Rival firms grudgingly matched it, then raised billable-hour targets and lengthened the partner track to afford it. Adjusted for inflation, that 1968 figure is worth roughly $145,000 today, well under the $235,000 base a Cravath first-year starts at now. 

See the answer on the next page. 

The post Where The ‘Cravath Scale’ Actually Began appeared first on Above the Law .
items.t: Where The ‘Cravath Scale’ Actually Began

items.title: ALERT: Cravath Makes Its Associate Compensation Move!
items.summary:
Well, there it is.

It’s finally happening! On Tuesday, Cravath announced its year-end bonuses, its special bonuses, and a new associate salary scale, all in one memo. That’s the same Cravath that has spent the better part of half a year letting the rest of Biglaw stew in its silence .

The new base salaries start at $235,000 for the class of 2026 and go up to $440,000 for the class of 2020. That matches the scale Milbank set when it kicked off the 2026 salary wars on June 2 . But Cravath’s new salaries take effect January 1, 2027, while Milbank’s took effect July 1.

Back in August, we floated the theory that Cravath might hold everything until bonus season. That way it could announce year-end bonuses, match Milbank’s specials, and unveil the new salary scale all at once, and get the last word.

Well. That’s exactly what happened.

Cravath also didn’t just match Milbank’s summer special bonuses . It came over the top. Milbank’s specials ran from $6,000 to $25,000. Cravath’s run from $11,000 (prorated) for the class of 2026 to $40,000 for the class of 2021 and more senior classes. Year-end bonuses stay on the same scale as last year : $15,000 (prorated) for the newest class, up to $115,000 for the class of 2019. Add it all up and the most senior associates are getting $155,000 in bonuses, up from $140,000 last year.

As usual at Cravath, there’s no billable-hour requirement. According to the memo, “virtually all our associates will receive the full bonuses.” New York and D.C. bonuses will be paid December 11, and London bonuses December 18. Associates have to still be at…

items.title: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?
items.summary:
(Photo by CRASH:candy/Flickr) 

AI is rearing its head in our courtrooms, and judges are having to decide what to make of it. Two recent decisions show a wrong way and a right way to do just that.

I recently wrote about a federal district court judge in Texas, Mark Pittman, who excoriated some attorneys because he thought they used AI to draft briefs. And because he didn’t like the arguments that they made. He labeled the lawyers lazy and called their arguments tortured. All before holding a hearing. It was my view that this was the wrong way to look at AI and those who use it. 

Then along came an opinion out of the federal district court for the Eastern District of Kentucky. To me, it represents the right and studied way for courts to view AI and its use. The judge there denied a motion to dismiss by a cop who allegedly relied on AI facial recognition, and only AI, to make an arrest. 

The cases are factually different. One involved lawyers using AI, the other a cop. But both turn on the same question: how should a court think about AI and its use by those appearing before it?

The Alleged Kentucky Facts 

A Black man entered a bank in Florence, Ky., and attempted to cash what appeared to be a fraudulent check. The bank refused to cash the check, and he left. A security camera captured an unobstructed view of his face. 

A local police department detective named Kilmer allegedly took a screenshot of the man’s face from the footage. He then used AI facial recognition technology to match that screenshot with a booking photo on file. The cop took the booking photo and a…
items.t: AI In Our Courts: Useful Or A Magic 8 Ball?

items.title: Where Should AI Expertise Live In Legal?
items.summary:
Getty Images 

Curt McDaniel and I have been talking about Legal Operations for a long time, and not just theoretically.

Before retiring in 2025, Curt spent 19 years at Ferring Pharmaceuticals, including six as Chief Legal Officer, where he led a significant evolution in how the global legal function delivered its services. Curt and I have spent years looking at Legal Operations from opposite sides of the table.  

Over the years, we’ve stayed in touch, and Curt and I still regularly compare notes about where the profession is headed. Not surprisingly, lately those conversations have included a lot of artificial intelligence “what-ifs.”

We agree on a lot, including that AI needs to be part of a broader legal strategy, not a standalone technology project.

But one question has generated more debate between us than most:

Where should AI expertise actually live inside Legal? 

My perspective is that Legal Ops may have to become the AI expert inside the legal department. As AI’s capabilities have evolved, so has Curt’s view. He sees a need for deep AI expertise in an in-house legal team, led by Legal Ops and supported by lawyers with some level of expertise.

Our discussion led us to ask: What kind of AI expertise does Legal Operations truly need? 

Legal Ops Shouldn’t Become IT 

Curt raises an important concern: AI isn’t a Legal-only technology. It cuts across the entire enterprise, and organizations already have teams responsible for technology, data, security, privacy, finance, and other areas critical to implementing it responsibly.

Legal can’t simply build its own AI…
items.t: Where Should AI Expertise Live In Legal?

The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

In United States v. Talbott , the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

In the government’s petition for review , U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. items.title: Death By A Thousand Cuts: Breaking An Already Broken Immigration System
items.summary:
Describing just how dysfunctional the U.S. immigration system has gotten is becoming increasingly difficult.

The headlines tell one story: immigrants detained, families separated, businesses reconsidering visa sponsorship, or being suspended from sponsoring altogether, and ever-changing policies creating widespread uncertainty.

But behind those headlines lies a much larger, largely invisible crisis: the immigration system itself is breaking down.

When people learn that I am an immigration attorney, they often say, “Wow, you must be busy!”

Yes, immigration lawyers are incredibly busy. But not necessarily doing the work we should be doing. Instead of helping employers recruit talent, and families reunite, we spend an extraordinary amount of time correcting government errors, troubleshooting dysfunctional filing systems, and navigating bureaucratic chaos.

We are busy doing busywork. 

And the consequences are far from trivial. Every administrative failure creates uncertainty, delays, additional costs, and sometimes life-altering consequences for the people and businesses depending on the system.

Here is what that looks like in practice.

1. Getting An Application Accepted Has Become An Obstacle Course 

In my 20 years practicing immigration law, simply getting an application accepted for filing has never been this difficult.

Applications are rejected over filing fees, payment processing, and technicalities, even when we follow published instructions.

The United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) frequently attributes payment failures to banks…
items.t: Death By A Thousand Cuts: Breaking An Already Broken Immigration System

items.title: Alito’s Long-Term Plan: Outlast Every Supreme Court Justice In History
items.summary:
Ed. note : Welcome to our daily feature, Quote of the Day . 

If I can hang on for five more years, I will reach 26th place. Ten years, 15th place. And in 16 years, if AI has not killed off humanity, I will have passed every former justice.

items.title: New Tool Seeks To Ease Burden On Government Watchdogs (To The Extent They Exist Anymore)
items.summary:
Running an inspector general’s office isn’t easy. For one thing, this administration will very likely just fire your whole office on a Friday night and replace you with a FedSoc chapter president coming off a Turning Point internship — if they bother to fill the positions at all . But all inspectors general work for the federal government. There are IGs up and down the system keeping agencies honest.

Casepoint just announced a new offering to make that job a little easier.

Casepoint Investigations is a workflow management product for inspector general and law enforcement offices at the federal, state, and local level, designed to keep intake, deadlines, evidence, and findings in a single record, running on the same platform as Casepoint’s eDiscovery product.

The release describes the status quo tech nightmare facing an IG office:

Investigations offices work under constantly evolving rules and workflows. When an executive order sets a new requirement, a state issues new guidance, or an oversight review uncovers a process gap, the process has to change with it. Many offices run workflows on homegrown systems built on SharePoint or internal spreadsheets, so changes are made by hand. Offices on legacy systems wait instead: a vendor engineer, a contract modification, budget approval, and weeks or months before anything changes. An office that simply wants to improve its own processes waits just as long.

Executive orders setting new requirements? I thought those were just meant to extort the nation’s most cowardly law firms .

items.title: Judge Orders Trump Administration To Produce The Biglaw Deals And The Emails Behind Them
items.summary:
The nine Biglaw firms that bent the knee to Donald Trump paid for one thing above all else: for it all to go away. Their deals came with roughly $940 million in pro bono payola for Trump-approved causes, and in exchange they thought they got peace, quiet, and nobody asking too many questions.

But reality is a harsh mistress like that. 

On Monday, U.S. District Judge Amir Ali granted a key records request in the American Bar Association’s suit over the administration’s “law firm intimidation policy.” According to Bloomberg Law, the White House now has to produce the agreements it struck with Paul Weiss, Kirkland, Skadden, Latham & Watkins, Milbank, A&O Shearman, Simpson Thacher, Willkie Farr, and Cadwalader (now part of Hogan Lovells Cadwalader). It also has to hand over its communications with those nine firms, plus communications with the smaller group of firms Trump went after with executive orders.

Ali ordered the administration to share communications relating to “any possible issuance of any executive order against any law firm, or to any agreement with any law firm and the government.” He limited the request to communications that took place between the start of Trump’s second term through June 2025.

The requested communications are “directly relevant” to whether the government issued retaliatory sanction threats that would have discouraged ABA members from engaging in activity protected by the First Amendment.

items.title: Salaries, Special Bonuses, And Year-End Bonuses On Point At Gibson Dunn
items.summary:
It’s a match! Actually, make that three matches! Gibson Dunn has announced it’s moving associates to the Milbank salary scale and paying both Milbank’s special bonuses and market-rate year-end bonuses.

Let’s start with base pay. Gibson associates are moving to the salary scale Milbank set back in June . It runs from $235,000 for first-years to $455,000 for the most senior associates. The new salaries take effect in 2027. 

But, wait! There’s more! Gibson is also matching Milbank’s summer special bonuses , which range from $6,000 to $25,000 depending on class year. On top of that come year-end bonuses from $20,000 to $115,000. The baby associates in the class of 2026 get $15,000, prorated, because a few months of Biglaw life doesn’t earn you the full freight. Put it all together and the most senior associates can take home $140,000 in bonuses, the same top-of-the-industry number floating about.

Check out the full grid below.

Notably, Cravath, the firm Biglaw has traditionally waited on before opening its checkbook, still hasn’t said a word . And Gibson can certainly afford it. The firm spent the summer collecting marquee litigators like Infinity Stones, landing Bill Savitt from Wachtell and Jeff Wall from Sullivan & Cromwell.

items.title: Litigation Boutique Makes Its Summer Program The Worst Deal In Town
items.summary:
Listen, law school recruiting is a mess, and everyone knows it. When NALP scrapped its decades-old recruiting guidelines back in 2018, the race to the bottom was on. Seven years later, Biglaw’s recruitment of law students is well and truly broken , and it’s worse for the students, the firms, and the law schools alike. 1Ls are securing their 2L summer jobs before their 1L summer jobs . Some firms are now skipping screening interviews entirely and sending 1Ls straight to callbacks before they’ve sat for a single law school exam. The competition for top-tier legal talent coming out of law school has gotten insane.

So when an elite firm announces it’s pushing back on the early-hiring frenzy, you’d expect to be cheering. But, oof, this is a choice.

San Francisco’s Keker, Van Nest & Peters will stop giving full-time offers to summer associates at the end of the summer, Reuters reports , and will instead have them apply for those jobs “when they are ready.” The change takes effect in 2028. Here’s how partner and hiring committee chair Sharif Jacob explained it:

“We believe it would be better for the associates and the firm if they just have a little bit more experience before they have to make these big decisions. So we’re encouraging that.”

This is absolutely not the way to push back on what’s wrong with law school recruitment.

Even before on-campus recruiting became a shadow of its former self, getting an offer after your 2L summer was the standard. That was the whole point of the summer program. If for some reason you didn’t get one, it was strange, because almost…

items.title: Thanks To AI, Baker McKenzie Wants To Break Up With The Billable Hour
items.summary:
The billable hour has survived plenty of predictions about its impending demise. But with artificial intelligence promising to speed up legal work, Biglaw firms are facing an increasingly awkward question: How do you keep charging for all those hours when the work takes less time?

Baker McKenzie is looking to change the conversation.

According to the Wall Street Journal ⁠, the firm is encouraging lawyers to make value-based billing the default, while retaining hourly billing where needed. Global chair Sunny Mann says AI is making time a less useful measure of legal services. “The hourly rate isn’t the right metric,” he said. “I think it’s a trend that you’ll see across the legal industry.”

For a profession that has built so much of its business around tracking six-minute increments, that’s a meaningful shift. Of course, moving away from hourly billing doesn’t mean Biglaw is suddenly embracing smaller profits. Let’s not get carried away. Mann sees AI’s efficiencies as an opportunity to bring in additional matters, with lower litigation costs potentially encouraging clients to head to court more often.

“Even if there’s more efficiency in the process and that volume of work may go down, I also then see a world in which clients will think, because it’s cheaper, we can litigate more,” he said.

More lawsuits. There’s a vision of the AI future that Biglaw can get behind.

As we’ve previously discussed ⁠, AI getting work done faster creates something of a dilemma for firms accustomed to charging by the hour. Clients may expect a smaller bill, while partners would prefer that…
items.t: Thanks To AI, Baker McKenzie Wants To Break Up With The Billable Hour

That said, we presume he knows these letters are meritless and is just using his taxpayer-funded office to inflate his MAGA Q-score, which is why he’s posting them all on X.

As one might imagine, the legal profession has many rules and regulations against exactly this behavior, which is why the Campaign for Accountability filed a grievance with the State Bar of Texas over Reitz’s Tweetstorm.

items.title: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once
items.summary:
On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

***

Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a) . According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado .

Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal…
items.t: Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

items.title: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently
items.summary:
Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy , on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy 

Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free…
items.t: Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

items.title: Key takeaways from Monday’s order list
items.summary:
Forty-six years ago today, the Supreme Court issued its ruling in Stone v. Graham , holding that a Kentucky statute requiring a copy of the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms violated the First Amendment’s establishment clause because it “has no secular legislative purpose.” That 1980 ruling is back in the spotlight this term, as the court considers whether to take up challenges to similar Ten Commandments laws in Texas and Louisiana .

At the Court On Monday, the Supreme Court denied review in dozens of cases, including two DEI-related disputes – the first, a challenge from University of California scholars to cuts in research funding; the second, a challenge from California doctors to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses – and a Second Amendment clash over Maryland laws prohibiting guns in “sensitive places.”

The court also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

For more on Monday’s order list , see the Morning Reads and On Site sections below.

The December session of oral arguments will begin on Nov. 30.
items.t: Key takeaways from Monday’s order list

items.title: ‘Nothing they said made sense’: down the rabbit hole with Britain’s sovereign citizens
items.summary:
It is an anti-government ideology that began in the US and has spread across the world – wasting public resources and ruining lives. But why have the wild ideas of this movement become so appealing?

In the early morning of 20 June 2023, 13 police officers raided a five-bed barn conversion in rural Hampshire. The occupant, a 57-year-old man named Iain Clifford Stamp, was rudely awoken. The police informed him that they were executing a warrant on behalf of the Financial Conduct Authority, the body that regulates financial services in the UK. FCA raids are rare. They are only permitted when the regulator can persuade a judge that there are reasonable grounds for believing the person or firm that they are investigating will not cooperate. In this case, it seems, there was good reason to believe that Iain Clifford Stamp might cause trouble.

Stamp’s frosty relationship with financial authorities dated back to 2008, when his first company, a financial product provider called Integrity, imploded and was left facing claims from clients of up to an estimated £80m. Back then, Integrity had been publicly censured by the Financial Services Authority for not fairly communicating to customers the risks in the products it was selling. This time was more serious.…

items.title: ‘He’s a master manipulator’: one woman’s fight against her abuser’s early release –podcast
items.summary:
The government is releasing criminals early to stop prisons being overcrowded. But where does that leave their victims? Helen Pidd speaks to a domestic abuse survivor about the release of her perpetrator – former Lancashire police detective, Michael Harvey.

items.title: Why Everything Looks Chaotic From The GC’s Desk
items.summary:
Imagine opening your inbox to a customer escalation, a product question, a contract exception, and a request for board materials. Each has a different owner. Each has a different deadline. All four need an answer today.

Now suppose they involve the same thing: the company has started describing an AI feature in a way its product documentation does not support.

Sales encounters the problem as a customer expectation. Product encounters it as an ambiguous requirement. Legal encounters it as contract language. The board encounters it as a question about oversight.

Four requests. One possible connection worth investigating.

That is the image behind a series I am calling “Above the Crossing.” Picture a GC standing amid the multidirectional movement of Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo. At street level, the most urgent task is avoiding the next collision. From a higher vantage point, routes and recurring points of convergence become easier to notice.

I use the image because a legal inbox organizes work by arrival. It offers very little help understanding how the work was produced.

A request that arrives on Thursday may have begun with a product decision made in February. Another request, arriving minutes later, may reflect a commercial commitment made yesterday. Their simultaneous arrival tells you almost nothing about their relationship.

Even the labels can get in the way. “Commercial,” “privacy,” and “product” are useful for assigning lawyers. They can separate matters that depend on the same fact, owner, or unresolved decision.

items.title: Realize Your Mistake Late — But Don’t Expect Us To Be Impressed
items.summary:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is a hoot.

She was the wokest of the woke a half-dozen years ago, leading the charge for Woke 1: Defund the police. Don’t prosecute shoplifters. Avoid microaggressions. Defend the term “woke” itself against attacks.

But now she’s realized that Woke 1 went too far: “ Woke 1 was crazy. “

You don’t say.

Congratulations, AOC! You’ve caught on. But I’d rather support someone who was intelligent enough to see the truth all along.

I’m not ideological about this; it cuts in all directions.

Although Megyn Kelly was hardly the worst, she was only too willing to spread misleading electoral narratives in 2020 and 2021. But now, when Donald Trump tries to pull the same stunt and insist that the 2026 elections were stolen, she tells him to “ Just stop. “

Do tell.

Congratulations, Megyn!  You’ve caught on. But I’d rather hear opinion commentary from someone who was intelligent enough to see the truth all along.

Michael Cohen thought that Trump was the cat’s meow. And then he thought that Trump was a criminal who threatened democracy. And now he again thinks that Trump was OK. And in five years, when Trump’s inexplicable luster has vanished, Cohen will change his mind yet again.

Do people really listen to clowns like this?

I promise you that, within five or 10 years, you’ll be hearing from Republicans telling you that they’ve realized that Trump was a clownish buffoon all along.

Is that a fact?

Congratulations, Republicans! You’ll have seen the light.

But why didn’t you realize that Trump was a clownish buffoon from the very start? Wasn’t it obvious…

items.title: Biglaw Skipping 1L Interviews And Going Straight To Callbacks Before First-Semester Exams
items.summary:
Law firms started throwing the hiring cycle into disarray a few years ago, blowing off the tried and true on-campus interviewing regime to start recruiting in the middle of the academic year. As students and law schools complained about the incursion, the firms upped the ante, beginning to interview future lawyers before students even take first-semester exams. 

Now we’re hearing that at least a couple firms have gone further, eschewing initial interviews altogether and jumping straight to callbacks based on nothing but an application and vibes. Meanwhile, students have to show up to class in suits so they can bolt the moment the lecture ends. Which isn’t necessarily new, but we used to do that the first month of 2L fall. Meanwhile these students have to do it with their very first law school exams coming as early as three weeks from now .

According to one T14 tipster, the decision to jump right to callbacks beginning as early as this month caught students completely unaware. In fact, students started receiving links to sign up for callbacks within a week of sending in their applications. 

Which sort of does violence to the word “call back .”

Biglaw recruiting has morphed into the doomsday machine from Dr. Strangelove . Everyone agrees it’s insane . Bloomberg Law literally titled a podcast episode “ Everyone Hates Early Law School Recruiting, But Everyone Does It .” Morgan Lewis chair Jami McKeon told the outlet the firm is “absolutely” recruiting students before their first exams: “That’s what the market is right now, so you have to do it.” [1]

He plans to discuss the current state of AI in general. And, according to the press release, what happens to evidence when realistic documents, photographs, and videos can be generated with a click.

We were joined in the interview session by Brian Ray . Ray is CSU Law’s co-interim dean, Baker Hostetler chair in law, and director of the Center for Cybersecurity and Privacy Protection . Ray knows a thing or two about AI himself.

items.title: Listening to the past
items.summary:
Originalism sometimes requires judges to sift a historical record to determine what the law is. That is because it holds that we should give the Constitution its original meaning, and the text of the Constitution does not always make that meaning readily apparent to modern readers.

In a column last year, I considered a common criticism of originalism: that judges make poor historians. Maybe, I concluded , but they can still be good (originalist) judges.

A related criticism of originalism is that history makes a poor judge. Judges must be decisive, but historical inquiry is often inconclusive. This month’s column considers this criticism – specifically, two common forms that it takes: (1) originalism attributes too much significance to historical silence, and (2) originalism cannot reconcile dissonant historical traditions.

The role of history in text-and-history cases 

Originalists turn to the historical record for a variety of purposes. Because originalism holds that the Constitution means today what it meant in 1789 (except to the extent that it has been lawfully amended), understanding the meaning of its words requires looking to historical sources to figure out how those words were used at the time the Constitution was ratified. To take an uncontroversial example, while a modern reader might read “domestic violence” and think “spousal abuse,” historical context reveals that “domestic Violence” in the guarantee clause means internal civil unrest.

Sometimes, however, originalists look to the historical record for purposes other than uncovering the contemporary…
items.t: Listening to the past

items.title: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket
items.summary:
Justice Samuel Alito sat for an interview with the Associated Press in early October about his new book, “ So Ordered .” In the book and the interview, he made three claims about the court’s emergency docket. First, applications on it now rival the number of cases the court decides after full briefing and oral argument. Second, this growth can be traced to presidents who govern by executive order, which produces lower-court rulings that move quickly to the Supreme Court. Third, he does not expect the trend to reverse. “Unless something changes there, and I don’t foresee it right now,” he said, “I’m afraid this is going to continue.” Alito added, such “[a]n application is something that I think we have to rule on.”

Readers of this column know I prefer data to anecdotes, even when the anecdotes come from a Supreme Court justice. The 2025-26 term, which ended on Oct. 4, provides the receipts. And the data support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.

The volume fell, but not to normal 

In the 2024-25 term, the Trump administration filed 27 substantive applications that reached the full court. In the 2025-26 term, it filed 12. Every other applicant held steady. States filed nine applications in the 2024-25 term and 8 last term, and private parties filed 19 and 20. The entire decline came from the executive branch.

For most of the past quarter century, the federal government rarely asked the court for such relief. It filed 6 applications across the 2000-01 through 2015-16 terms, never more than one in a single term. That changed during the first Trump…
items.t: “I’m afraid this is going to continue”: Justice Alito, the executive, and the emergency docket

items.title: How I survived being forced into pornography: ‘I died in that hotel room. I was a walking corpse’
items.summary:
In 2016, Mariah Rief, then 19, thought she was going to a modelling job at a hotel. Once there, she was sex trafficked. She knows of 15 fellow victims who have since died by suicide or drug overdose – and is determined to stop it ever happening again

When people ask Mariah Rief about her experience as a survivor of sex trafficking, they tend to start with the Craigslist ad which led the then 19-year-old to a “modelling shoot” at the Hilton hotel in San Diego. For others, the story starts when Rief enters the lobby and meets Theodore Gyi, the “photographer”. Or after they’ve taken the elevator up to a room, Rief standing at the threshold, Gyi behind her blocking her exit – and just inside the door, the silhouette of a second man waiting.

Whenever she talks about it, and whatever the questions, Rief always braces herself for blame, because, to some, it makes no sense. “You get, ‘But why did she answer that ad?’ ‘Why did she walk inside?’ and, my favourite, ‘Where were her parents?’” says Rief. “If you live in an idyllic world, it’s hard to imagine how this could happen.” The true starting point is years earlier. Rief’s beginnings, her childhood, layers of trauma and chaos, fast-tracked her to that hotel room in November 2016, believing that finally, life might be giving her a break. “It’s painful to say it but I was truly the perfect victim,” she says. “I saw that job as an opportunity. When I arrived at that hotel, I thought I was so lucky.”
items.t: How I survived being forced into pornography: ‘I died in that hotel room. I was a walking corpse’

In a brief list of orders from their private conference earlier in the day, the justices announced that it will review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that struck down the policy as an overreach by the government. The court also added a second case involving the standard for securities-fraud cases to its oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term.

The asylum case is the latest addition to the court’s burgeoning immigration docket , which already includes a challenge to the Trump administration’s practice of deporting immigrants to countries that are not identified in their removal orders (a policy known as “third-party removals”) and its policy of detaining immigrants who are apprehended within the United States without the opportunity for a hearing.

Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services has its roots in a Jan. 20, 2025, proclamation by President Donald Trump declaring that “an invasion is ongoing at the southern border” and suspending (that is, temporarily blocking) the entry of noncitizens “engaged in the invasion.” Trump also indicated that such noncitizens could no longer seek protections, such as asylum, that would allow them to remain in the country.

items.t: Supreme Court agrees to hear case on Trump administration’s suspension of asylum

items.title: This term is not just short on blockbuster cases. It’s short on cases, period.
items.summary:
As the 2026-27 term got underway this fall, several commentators observed that it was shaping up to be a quiet term compared to the one before it. There are important disputes tied to climate change , immigration , and the Second Amendment . But no case is quite comparable to last term’s battles over tariffs , birthright citizenship , executive authority , and the Voting Rights Act .

Just over a month later, the oral argument docket still remains relatively short on blockbuster cases. Perhaps of even greater note, though, is that it’s short on cases in general, as the court is running behind its typical pace for grants.
items.t: This term is not just short on blockbuster cases. It’s short on cases, period.

items.title: Tribal property and the Supreme Court
items.summary:
One of the fundamental questions in federal law is the exact parameters of Indigenous property rights. From the first Supreme Court decisions in Indian affairs (such as Johnson v. McIntosh and Lone Wolf v. Hitchcock ) , Indigenous property has been treated in a sui generis manner that is often to the detriment of Indigenous Peoples. Bryan Newland, assistant secretary for Indian Affairs in the Biden administration, recently delivered a major address in which he explained that the legacy of cases decided in the “ atmosphere ” of colonization remain impactful in 21st century litigation.

Before the court is a petition to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit’s decision in Chase v. Andeavor Logistics LP (now captioned Aubol v. Andeavor Logistics LP ), a trespass action by tribal citizen allotment owners against a pipeline company. Allotments are land parcels carved out of Indian reservations in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. The federal right-of-way allowing a pipeline in these Indigenous lands expired in 2013. The Mandan, Hidatsa, and Arikara Nation has agreed to extend the right-of-way for its lands, but individual tribal citizens have not consented to the extension on their lands.

Though the pipeline company is seemingly liable for trespass, the circuit court remanded the issue to the Bureau of Indian Affairs to address the issue in the first instance, pointing to federal regulations that govern the expiration of Indian country rights-of-way. The cert petition argues that the 8th Circuit’s decision conflicts with the Supreme Court’s decision in…
items.t: Tribal property and the Supreme Court

items.title: The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS
items.summary:
The Supreme Court heard three oral arguments this week, wrapping up the November argument session. It also decided an interim docket case on border wall construction in southwestern Texas, granting the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to continue construction in an apparent 8-1 vote.

At the Court This Week Today, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review . Orders from today’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from James Pavatt, who was sentenced to death for the 2001 murder of Rob Andrew. Just over an hour later, Pavatt was executed in Oklahoma.

On Tuesday, the justices heard oral argument in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards, LLC , on whether the Constitution allows the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – to adjudicate an employer’s obligation to comply with employment agreements concerning temporary immigrant workers. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis .

On Monday, the justices heard argument in Nielsen v. Watanabe , on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for constitutional violations. Here are the links to our Case Preview and Argument Analysis .

items.t: The major Trump cases that might come back to SCOTUS
